title: Eliminate Accidental Cartesian Products in Joins
description_markdown: Optimize a query joining `departments` and `projects`: ensure the join connects strictly on `d.dept_id = p.dept_id`. Return `d.dept_name` and `p.project_name` for projects with budget >= 500,000. Order by `d.dept_name` ASC, `p.project_name` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Explicit INNER JOIN predicate
SELECT ...
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, p.project_name FROM departments d JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id WHERE p.budget >= 500000 ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, p.project_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Explicit join predicates allow Hash Join or Merge Join planner nodes, avoiding catastrophic $O(N \times M)$ nested loop scans.

solution_explanation: EXISTS short-circuits upon the first matching index leaf entry, outperforming COUNT(*) > 0 which scans entire tables.

title: Apply SARGable Boundary Filtering to Calendar Date Columns
description_markdown: Write an index-friendly (SARGable) query to find all employees hired in calendar year 2021 without wrapping `hire_date` in any function. Use the half-open range `hire_date >= '2021-01-01' AND hire_date < '2022-01-01'`. Return `emp_id`, `first_name`, and `hire_date`. Order by `hire_date` ASC, `emp_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- SARGable date filtering
SELECT emp_id, first_name, hire_date
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date >= '2021-01-01' AND hire_date < '2022-01-01'
ORDER BY hire_date ASC, emp_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT emp_id, first_name, hire_date FROM employees WHERE hire_date >= '2021-01-01' AND hire_date < '2022-01-01' ORDER BY hire_date ASC, emp_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Wrapping indexed columns in functions (e.g. EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date)) prevents B-tree index seek access.
common_mistakes: Using YEAR(hire_date) = 2021 which breaks SARGability.
interview_tip: Always write date boundaries as half-open intervals >= start AND < end to enable index range scans.
hints: Query: SELECT emp_id, first_name, hire_date FROM employees WHERE hire_date >= '2021-01-01' AND hire_date < '2022-01-01' ORDER BY hire_date ASC, emp_id ASC;

title: Optimize Text Search with Prefix-Only LIKE Wildcards
description_markdown: Perform an index-friendly prefix search to find products whose name begins with 'Coffee' using `product_name LIKE 'Coffee%'`. Avoid leading wildcards. Return `product_id`, `product_name`, and `price`. Order by `product_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Index-friendly prefix LIKE search
SELECT product_id, product_name, price
FROM products
WHERE product_name LIKE 'Coffee%'
ORDER BY product_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT product_id, product_name, price FROM products WHERE product_name LIKE 'Coffee%' ORDER BY product_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Prefix patterns like 'Coffee%' utilize standard B-Tree index scans, whereas '%Coffee%' forces full table scans.
common_mistakes: Using '%Coffee%' which negates index seek benefits.
interview_tip: Leading wildcards defeat B-Tree index lookup because leaf nodes are sorted left-to-right.
hints: Query: SELECT product_id, product_name, price FROM products WHERE product_name LIKE 'Coffee%' ORDER BY product_id ASC;

title: Isolate Arithmetic Calculations to Right Hand Side of Predicates
description_markdown: Write an optimized SARGable filter to locate employees earning at least 100,000 (`salary >= 100000`). Keep the column alone on the left-hand side of the comparison operator. Return `emp_id`, `first_name`, and `salary`. Order by `salary` DESC, `emp_id` ASC.

title: Construct Null-Safe High-Performance Anti-Join via NOT EXISTS
description_markdown: Find customers who have never placed any orders using an efficient `NOT EXISTS` anti-join rather than `NOT IN`. Return `customer_id`, `first_name`, and `email`. Order by `customer_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- NOT EXISTS anti-join
SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.email FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC;
solution_explanation: NOT EXISTS avoids NOT IN three-valued logic null traps and transforms cleanly into Hash Anti-Joins.
common_mistakes: Using NOT IN on columns that could contain NULL values.
interview_tip: NOT EXISTS is universally preferred over NOT IN for safety and query planner optimization.
hints: Use `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)`.
Query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.email FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC;

title: Eliminate Unnecessary Deduplication Overhead with UNION ALL
description_markdown: Combine customers from 'Seattle' with customers from 'London' using `UNION ALL` to bypass expensive distinct hashing or sorting passes between naturally disjoint sets. Return `customer_id`, `first_name`, and `city`. Order by `customer_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- High-performance UNION ALL
SELECT customer_id, first_name, city FROM customers WHERE city = 'Seattle'
UNION ALL
SELECT customer_id, first_name, city FROM customers WHERE city = 'London'
ORDER BY customer_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT customer_id, first_name, city FROM customers WHERE city = 'Seattle' UNION ALL SELECT customer_id, first_name, city FROM customers WHERE city = 'London' ORDER BY customer_id ASC;
solution_explanation: UNION performs a costly Sort or Unique Hash operation, whereas UNION ALL streams results directly without overhead.
common_mistakes: Using plain UNION when the datasets are known to have zero overlap.
interview_tip: Always choose UNION ALL unless distinct deduplication is an explicit business requirement.
hints: Use `UNION ALL` between the two SELECT statements.
Query: SELECT customer_id, first_name, city FROM customers WHERE city = 'Seattle' UNION ALL SELECT customer_id, first_name, city FROM customers WHERE city = 'London' ORDER BY customer_id ASC;

description_markdown: From `customers`, filter for `country = 'USA'`. Explicitly project only the three necessary columns `customer_id`, `first_name`, and `email`, avoiding wasteful `SELECT *` over-fetching. Order by `customer_id` ASC.

solution_explanation: Requesting only required columns enables index-only covering scans and minimizes memory transfer bandwidth.

title: Optimize Top-1 Per Group Using Single-Pass Window Function
description_markdown: Using a single-pass window function (`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id ASC) AS rn`), find the highest-paid employee in each department where `dept_id IS NOT NULL`. Filter for `rn = 1`. Return `emp_id`, `dept_id`, `first_name`, and `salary`. Order by `dept_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Single-pass Top-1 per group
SELECT emp_id, dept_id, first_name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT emp_id, dept_id, first_name, salary,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id ASC) AS rn
  FROM employees
  WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
) sub
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY dept_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT emp_id, dept_id, first_name, salary FROM (SELECT emp_id, dept_id, first_name, salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id ASC) AS rn FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL) sub WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY dept_id ASC;
solution_explanation: ROW_NUMBER() finds the top record per group in a single streaming sort, vastly outperforming quadratic correlated subqueries.
common_mistakes: Writing correlated subqueries where salary = (SELECT MAX(...) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = e1.dept_id).
interview_tip: Top-N per group via ROW_NUMBER replaces $O(N^2)$ correlated subqueries with an efficient $O(N \log N)$ single pass.
hints: Compute `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id ASC) AS rn` in derived table.

Query: SELECT emp_id, dept_id, first_name, salary FROM (SELECT emp_id, dept_id, first_name, salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id ASC) AS rn FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL) sub WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY dept_id ASC;

title: Include Primary Key in Grouping to Leverage Functional Dependency
description_markdown: Join `departments d` and `employees e` with `LEFT JOIN` on `d.dept_id = e.dept_id`. Group by `d.dept_id, d.dept_name` to exploit functional dependency on the primary key, and calculate `COUNT(e.emp_id) AS employee_count`. Return `d.dept_name` and `employee_count`. Order by `employee_count` DESC, `d.dept_name` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Group by primary key with dependency
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS employee_count
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name
ORDER BY employee_count DESC, d.dept_name ASC;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS employee_count FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY employee_count DESC, d.dept_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Grouping by primary key (dept_id) ensures strict hash grouping efficiency and satisfies ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY requirements.
common_mistakes: Using COUNT(*) which would count 1 for empty departments in a LEFT JOIN.
interview_tip: COUNT(e.emp_id) correctly yields 0 when a department contains no assigned employees.
hints: Query: SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS employee_count FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY employee_count DESC, d.dept_name ASC;

title: Implement Keyset Pagination via Seek Predicates Over Large Offsets
description_markdown: Fetch the next page of 5 orders after `order_id = 10` using keyset pagination (`WHERE order_id > 10`) rather than expensive `OFFSET` scanning. Return `order_id`, `order_date`, and `total_amount`. Order by `order_id` ASC with `LIMIT 5`.
starter_query:
-- Keyset seek pagination
SELECT order_id, order_date, total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE order_id > 10
ORDER BY order_id ASC
LIMIT 5;
solution_query: SELECT order_id, order_date, total_amount FROM orders WHERE order_id > 10 ORDER BY order_id ASC LIMIT 5;
solution_explanation: Keyset (seek-method) pagination performs an immediate index direct seek instead of scanning and discarding skipped rows.
common_mistakes: Using OFFSET 10 LIMIT 5 which forces the engine to read and discard all prior records.
interview_tip: Keyset pagination remains $O(1)$ constant time regardless of page depth, whereas OFFSET degrades to $O(N)$.
hints: Query: SELECT order_id, order_date, total_amount FROM orders WHERE order_id > 10 ORDER BY order_id ASC LIMIT 5;

title: Apply Early Predicate Filtering Prior to Multi-Table Joins
description_markdown: Filter employees in an inline derived query for `salary >= 120000` before joining with `departments d` on `dept_id`. Return `e.emp_id`, `e.first_name`, and `d.dept_name`. Order by `e.emp_id` ASC.

SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, d.dept_name

title: Apply Composite Filter Selectivity to Maximize Index Pruning
description_markdown: For completed orders (`order_status = 'completed'`) where `total_amount >= 200`, calculate a 10% promotional discount using `ROUND(total_amount * 0.90, 2)` as `discounted_amount`. Return `order_id`, `total_amount`, and `discounted_amount`. Order by `order_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Selective composite filtering
SELECT order_id, total_amount, ROUND(total_amount * 0.90, 2) AS discounted_amount

WHERE order_status = 'completed' AND total_amount >= 200
ORDER BY order_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT order_id, total_amount, ROUND(total_amount * 0.90, 2) AS discounted_amount FROM orders WHERE order_status = 'completed' AND total_amount >= 200 ORDER BY order_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Combining high-selectivity equality conditions with range checks leverages composite index structures.

hints: Query: SELECT order_id, total_amount, ROUND(total_amount * 0.90, 2) AS discounted_amount FROM orders WHERE order_status = 'completed' AND total_amount >= 200 ORDER BY order_id ASC;

title: Structure Discrete Categorical Alternatives Using IN Lists
description_markdown: From `employees`, filter for engineering titles using an explicit `IN` list: `job_title IN ('Software Engineer', 'Senior Software Engineer')`. Return `emp_id`, `first_name`, and `job_title`. Order by `emp_id` ASC.

title: Pre-Filter Datasets in WHERE Clause Prior to GROUP BY Aggregation
description_markdown: Count completed orders (`order_status = 'completed'`) per customer as `completed_orders`. Apply the status filter in the `WHERE` clause before `GROUP BY customer_id`. Return `customer_id` and `completed_orders`. Order by `completed_orders` DESC, `customer_id` ASC.

ORDER BY completed_orders DESC, customer_id ASC;

title: Apply Post-Aggregation Thresholds Efficiently in HAVING Clause
description_markdown: Join `students s` and `enrollments e` on `student_id`. Group by `s.student_id, s.first_name`. Filter for students enrolled in at least 2 courses (`HAVING COUNT(e.enrollment_id) >= 2`) as `course_count`. Return `s.student_id`, `s.first_name`, and `course_count`. Order by `course_count` DESC, `s.student_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Post-aggregation HAVING filter
SELECT s.student_id, s.first_name, COUNT(e.enrollment_id) AS course_count
FROM students s
JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id
GROUP BY s.student_id, s.first_name
HAVING COUNT(e.enrollment_id) >= 2
ORDER BY course_count DESC, s.student_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT s.student_id, s.first_name, COUNT(e.enrollment_id) AS course_count FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id GROUP BY s.student_id, s.first_name HAVING COUNT(e.enrollment_id) >= 2 ORDER BY course_count DESC, s.student_id ASC;
solution_explanation: HAVING filters groups post-aggregation after the GROUP BY hash table is populated.
common_mistakes: Trying to filter aggregate metrics in WHERE.
interview_tip: Group by primary key columns to permit safe projection of non-aggregate attributes.
hints: Query: SELECT s.student_id, s.first_name, COUNT(e.enrollment_id) AS course_count FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id GROUP BY s.student_id, s.first_name HAVING COUNT(e.enrollment_id) >= 2 ORDER BY course_count DESC, s.student_id ASC;

title: Execute Bounded Range Scan on Project Financial Budgets

solution_query: SELECT project_id, project_name, budget FROM projects WHERE budget BETWEEN 200000 AND 600000 ORDER BY budget DESC, project_id ASC;

hints: Query: SELECT project_id, project_name, budget FROM projects WHERE budget BETWEEN 200000 AND 600000 ORDER BY budget DESC, project_id ASC;

title: Prune Settlement Transactions Using High-Selectivity Multi-Condition Filtering

title: Safely Handle NULL Values in Left Join Aggregates with COALESCE
description_markdown: Join `departments d` and `employees e` using `LEFT JOIN` on `dept_id`. Group by `d.dept_id, d.dept_name, d.budget`. Calculate total department payroll, wrapping in `COALESCE(SUM(e.salary), 0)` as `total_payroll` to ensure zero is reported for unstaffed departments. Return `d.dept_id`, `d.dept_name`, `d.budget`, and `total_payroll`. Order by `d.dept_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Safe COALESCE aggregate rollups
SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name, d.budget, COALESCE(SUM(e.salary), 0) AS total_payroll
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name, d.budget
ORDER BY d.dept_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name, d.budget, COALESCE(SUM(e.salary), 0) AS total_payroll FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name, d.budget ORDER BY d.dept_id ASC;
solution_explanation: COALESCE prevents NULL values from escaping into application layers when LEFT JOINs have no right-side matches.
common_mistakes: Omitting COALESCE, allowing NULL to be returned instead of 0.
interview_tip: Always coalesce sums in outer joins to maintain consistent numeric reporting.
hints: Query: SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name, d.budget, COALESCE(SUM(e.salary), 0) AS total_payroll FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name, d.budget ORDER BY d.dept_id ASC;

title: Push Dimension Filtering into the Outer Join ON Clause
description_markdown: Join `customers c` and `orders o` using `LEFT JOIN` on `c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.order_status = 'completed'`. By placing `o.order_status = 'completed'` in the `ON` clause, all customers are retained while only completed orders are summed. Group by `c.customer_id, c.first_name`, and calculate `COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0) AS total_spent`. Return `c.customer_id`, `c.first_name`, and `total_spent`. Order by `total_spent` DESC, `c.customer_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Filter in outer join ON clause
SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.order_status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name
ORDER BY total_spent DESC, c.customer_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0) AS total_spent FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.order_status = 'completed' GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name ORDER BY total_spent DESC, c.customer_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Filtering the right table in the ON clause preserves all left table records, whereas filtering in WHERE converts the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
common_mistakes: Placing WHERE o.order_status = 'completed' in the WHERE clause, which accidentally eliminates customers without completed orders.
interview_tip: Understanding the crucial semantic and performance difference between filtering in ON vs WHERE is a senior SQL hallmark.
hints: Place `AND o.order_status = 'completed'` inside the LEFT JOIN ON clause.

Query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0) AS total_spent FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.order_status = 'completed' GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name ORDER BY total_spent DESC, c.customer_id ASC;
